summary:
Once a day is followed by a day with a higher-or-equal price, any later streak that reaches the earlier day also
covers the later one, so the earlier day never needs to be checked on its own again. Keep a stack of
(price, streak) pairs with strictly falling prices; a new price pops every pair it's at least as high as and
adds their streaks to 1. Amortised O(1) per call.

question.md:
Each `record(price)` adds the next day and returns its streak: the number of consecutive days ending today
(including today) with price **at most** today's.

- **"At most" includes equal prices**: equal days extend the streak.
- **The first day's streak is 1**, as is any day after a higher price.
- **Up to 10⁵ calls**, so a call can't afford to look at every past day.

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- "At most" includes equal prices: an equal earlier price extends the streak.
- The first day's streak is 1.
- Up to 10⁵ calls, so each must be fast on average.

think.md:
**The monotonic stack idea.** Keep a stack of items that are still **waiting for an answer** (for example "the next
warmer day"). When a new item arrives, it answers every waiting item it beats; those are popped. Because each popped
item was beaten by the new one, the items left on the stack are always in sorted order (that's the "monotonic" part),
so the new item only needs to look at the top.

**Why it's O(n).** Every item is pushed once and popped at most once, so all the `while` loops together do at most
`n` pops, even though a single step may pop many.

**Absorbing earlier days.** When today's price is at least an earlier day's price, today's streak covers that
day **and everything that day's streak covered**. So once a day is covered, it never needs to be looked at again:
store `(price, streak)` pairs on a stack and fold covered days into today's streak. Recording `[7, 3, 4, 4, 8, 2, 9]`:

approaches.title: Store every price, count backwards

idea.md: Store every price; for each new price, walk backwards counting days until one is higher.

build: Count backwards until a higher price.

lines.text: Walk back from today, counting days.
A higher price ends the streak.

complexity.md: **Time O(n)** per call in the worst case, O(n²) total. **Space O(n).**

steps.text: record(7): counting back from day 0, days 0..0 are ≤ 7. Streak 1.
record(3): counting back from day 1, days 1..1 are ≤ 3; day 0 (7) is higher. Streak 1.
record(4): counting back from day 2, days 1..2 are ≤ 4; day 0 (7) is higher. Streak 2.
record(4): counting back from day 3, days 1..3 are ≤ 4; day 0 (7) is higher. Streak 3.
record(8): counting back from day 4, days 0..4 are ≤ 8. Streak 5.
record(2): counting back from day 5, days 5..5 are ≤ 2; day 4 (8) is higher. Streak 1.
record(9): counting back from day 6, days 0..6 are ≤ 9. Streak 7.

walk.title: Keep every price. On each record, count backwards from today while prices are at most today's.

limits.md: Rising prices make every call walk the whole history. Absorbed days never need to be walked again.

approaches.title: Stack of (price, streak) pairs

idea.md:
Keep a stack of `(price, streak)`. For a new price, start at 1 and pop every pair with price `≤` today's,
adding its streak. Push `(price, streak)` and return the streak.

**Invariant.** Prices on the stack strictly decrease from bottom to top, and each pair's streak counts the
days it absorbed.

build: Pop and add streaks of pairs with price ≤ today's.

lines.text: Pairs (price, streak), prices strictly falling from bottom to top.

notes.java: `ArrayDeque` used as a stack: `push`, `peek` and `pop` work at the same end.

lines.text: A pair on top with price ≤ today's: its whole streak is ≤ its price ≤ today's, so it all joins today's streak. Its days are now represented by today's pair.
Today's pair goes on top; the price below it (if any) is strictly higher.

complexity.md: **Time O(1)** amortised per call (each day is pushed once and popped once). **Space O(n).**

steps.text: record(7): the top's price is higher (or there is none): streak 1.
record(3): the top's price is higher (or there is none): streak 1.
record(4): absorb ['3×1'] (price×streak), so the streak is 1 + 1 = 2.
record(4): absorb ['4×2'] (price×streak), so the streak is 1 + 2 = 3.
record(8): absorb ['4×3', '7×1'] (price×streak), so the streak is 1 + 3 + 1 = 5.
record(2): the top's price is higher (or there is none): streak 1.
record(9): absorb ['2×1', '8×5'] (price×streak), so the streak is 1 + 1 + 5 = 7.

walk.title: Keep a stack of (price, streak) pairs with strictly falling prices. A new price swallows every pair with a price at most its own, adding their streaks to its own.

takeaways.md:
- **Stock span:** stack of (price, span) pairs; a new price absorbs smaller-or-equal ones.
- Storing the span with each pair lets one pop stand for many days.
- **Pitfall:** using `<` when equal prices should count.
